phrases.translation: Ḥâ-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with the disjoint letters Ḥā Mīm. No fresh analysis of them is offered here, since their explanation has already been given earlier in the commentary and is not repeated. The text passes straight to the oath that follows, where God swears by the clear Book He sent down.

phrases.translation: By the clear Book
phrases.explanation: The verse is an oath. God swears by the Book He sent down on His Prophet, and the oath honours the revelation and presents it as evidence for what follows. Whoever reflects on its lessons and admonitions finds it guiding him to the right path and proving that it comes from One All-Wise and Praiseworthy, not from a human author or a lie.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We sent it down on a blessed night,
phrases.explanation: The Book is described as sent down by God on a night He calls blessed. The scholars named different nights. Some said it is the Night of Decree in Ramadan, and reports note that earlier scriptures also came down in that month. One report says the Quran was brought down as a whole on that night and then sent down to the prophets over time. Others named the middle of Sha'bān.

phrases.translation: for We always warn ˹against evil˺
phrases.explanation: The clause states the purpose of sending the Book. God sent it down as a warning, so that the punishment He has prepared falls only on those who reject what came to them and refuse to return to worshipping Him alone. This is also the argument for taking the blessed night as the Night of Decree, since warning and the sending down of the Book belong together.

phrases.translation: On that night
phrases.explanation: The pronoun points back to the blessed night just mentioned, so the disagreement about which night it is carries over here. The preferred view is that it is the Night of Decree. On it the affairs of the coming year are settled, who will die, who will be born, who is raised and who is lowered, along with provision and appointed terms.

phrases.translation: every matter of wisdom is ordained
phrases.explanation: Every firmly decreed matter is separated and made distinct on that night. The word rendered wise carries the sense of firmly decreed, as in the phrase the wise Book, which means the Book whose contents are settled. Reports describe the year being decided then, including who will die and who will be born. One report adds that the register of the blessed and the wretched is fixed, while provision and trials may be advanced or deferred.

phrases.translation: by a command from Us,
phrases.explanation: The settling of the year's affairs is described as a command that issues from God. The grammarians disputed how the word command is grammatically placed. Some from Kufa read it as a circumstance describing the sending down, so that the Book came down as a command and a mercy. Some from Basra attached it to the decree, so that every matter is distinguished by His command. Both readings lead to the same sense.

phrases.translation: for We have always sent ˹messengers˺
phrases.explanation: The closing words describe a settled practice. God has not left people without messengers, and the sending of the Prophet to his people belongs to that long sequence of warning. The same sentence continues into the next verse, where the sending is called a mercy from the Lord. Read together, the night, the decree and the messengers all serve one purpose, that people be warned before they are judged.

phrases.translation: as a mercy from your Lord.
phrases.explanation: The sending of the messenger is described as mercy, and the phrase explains why God has always sent warners. The word stands in the accusative because the sending governs it, so the mercy is attached to the one sent. The messenger is himself a mercy to the people he is sent to, since through him they learn what God asks of them and what awaits them.

phrases.translation: He ˹alone˺ is truly the All-Hearing, All-Knowing—
phrases.explanation: God hears everything the doubters say about the Book and about the messengers sent to them, and He knows what their hearts conceal. The two names close the sentence and frame the argument that follows. Nothing said against the revelation escapes His notice, and nothing hidden in a person's chest is absent from His knowledge. Neither the spoken denial nor the doubt behind it is lost.

phrases.translation: the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between,
phrases.explanation: The reciters disagreed over how this phrase is inflected, some joining it to the names just before it and some to the words your Lord earlier in the sentence. Both readings are well known and correct, and the meaning is the same either way. The One who sent down the Book and sent the messenger owns the heavens, the earth and everything between them.

phrases.translation: if only you had sure faith
phrases.explanation: The condition challenges the hearers rather than doubting them. If you are certain that your Lord owns the heavens and the earth, then you should be equally certain that the Book comes from Him and that the messenger speaks for Him. Certainty about the order of the world should carry over to what you are told about God, since both rest on the same Lord.

phrases.translation: There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him.
phrases.explanation: No being other than the Lord of the heavens and the earth deserves worship, and so worship is owed to Him alone. The verse turns the description of the previous verse into a demand. Since He alone owns all that exists, no other being can be served as He is served. The idols the people turned to can neither harm nor benefit them, and the verse excludes them.

phrases.translation: He ˹alone˺ gives life and causes death. ˹He is˺ your Lord, and the Lord of your forefathers
phrases.explanation: Life and death are in His hand alone, since He gives life to whatever He wills and causes to die whatever He wills of the living. The verse then names Him as Lord of the present generation and of the forefathers who passed before them. Their ancestors were owned by Him just as they are, so the worship He asks is not a new claim on them. The gods they served instead had no share in any of it.

phrases.translation: In fact, they are in doubt, amusing themselves
phrases.explanation: The verse answers the argument by naming the real condition of the hearers. They are not convinced by what is said to them and by what they are told about the Book, but they are in doubt. Rather than examining the doubt, they turn it into amusement. The verse names them as the polytheists of Quraysh, who play with the very matter that should concern them most.

phrases.translation: Wait then ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: The command answers the mockery of the previous verse. The Prophet is told to wait and watch for what will come to these people. The word carries the sense of watching for someone, and it places the dispute in God's hands rather than in the Prophet's. He is not asked to argue further or to force the matter, only to wait for the outcome that God has already announced.

phrases.translation: for the day ˹when˺ the sky will be veiled in haze, clearly visible
phrases.explanation: Two answers were given about this smoke. One report treats it as the famine that struck the Quraysh after the Prophet prayed against them, when hunger made them see smoke between them and the sky. Another treats it as a sign before the Hour that will seize people by the hearing. The first is preferred, since the verse threatens the Quraysh of that moment, but both reports may be true.

phrases.translation: overwhelming the people. ˹They will cry,˺ “This is a painful torment
phrases.explanation: The smoke covers the people, and the explanation given is that it covers their eyes through the sheer weight of what they suffer. Out of that distress they cry that this is a painful punishment. The words are put in their mouths by the verse, and the speaker is left unstated because the sense is plain. The verse moves from describing the affliction to quoting the confession it forces from them.

phrases.translation: Our Lord! Remove ˹this˺ torment from us, ˹and˺ we will certainly believe.”
phrases.explanation: The afflicted disbelievers turn to their Lord, asking that the punishment be lifted from them. They add a promise that if it is removed they will believe in Him and worship Him alone. This is presented as the prayer of people driven by hardship rather than by conviction. Their own later relapse is what the following verse reports, so the promise is recorded and then answered.

phrases.translation: How can they be reminded when a messenger has already come to them, making things clear
phrases.explanation: The question presses the point of the previous verses. Reminder will not help them once the affliction has arrived, since a messenger had already come to them and they turned away. They took no warning from the Book recited to them and no lesson from the proofs offered. The verse asks how admonition could reach people who refused it while it was still useful.

phrases.translation: then they turned away from him, saying, “A madman, taught by others!”
phrases.explanation: The reports give the verse a plain sense. They turned away from the Prophet and dismissed him as a madman who had been taught by others. The two charges answer different worries, one attacking his mind and the other his source. The verse records both without answering them here, since the reminder they refused and the punishment they mocked are its real subject.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We will remove ˹that˺ torment for a while,
phrases.explanation: God answers the promise by announcing that the affliction will be lifted for a short time. He does it through the plenty He restores to them, not because they deserve it. The lifting is temporary by design. Those who held that the smoke was a future sign said the punishment being removed is that smoke, and one report says it was already lifted when it appeared among them.

phrases.translation: and you ˹Meccans˺ will return ˹to disbelief˺
phrases.explanation: The second half removes any doubt about their sincerity. Once the hardship passes they will go back to what they were, breaking the promise made under pressure. One report reads the return as a return to God's punishment rather than to disbelief, which comes to the same end. The verse sets up the next one, where the seizing follows the relapse.

phrases.translation: ˹Then˺ on the Day We will deal ˹you˺ the fiercest blow,
phrases.explanation: The verse announces the consequence of relapsing. If the punishment is lifted and they return to their denial, God will take vengeance on the day of the great seizing, and it is read as a seizure in this worldly life that destroyed them. The reports differ over which day is meant. Many name the day of Badr, when the Quraysh were struck down.

phrases.translation: We will surely inflict punishment
phrases.explanation: Others read the great seizing as God's seizure of His enemies on the Day of Resurrection, and the reasons for the other view have already been given elsewhere. The closing words confirm that the seizing is an act of vengeance, not a random disaster. It answers the mockery recorded earlier in the surah, where the doubters played with the warning. The verse leaves the punishment firmly in God's hands.

phrases.translation: Indeed, before them We tested Pharaoh’s people:
phrases.explanation: The surah turns to an earlier people who met the same warning. Before the Quraysh, God tested the people of Pharaoh, the Copts, and the testing came through a messenger rather than through disaster alone. The story is offered as a pattern. Those who rejected Moses were not the first to hear a warning, and their fate answers the confidence of those who reject the Prophet.

phrases.translation: a noble messenger came to them
phrases.explanation: The messenger is Moses, as the reports state. He is called noble, and two reasons are given that may both hold. He was noble before God and held an exalted place with Him, or he was eminent among his people and of high lineage. Either way the description honours the one they rejected, so that their rejection is measured against the worth of the one sent to them.

phrases.translation: ˹proclaiming,˺ “Hand over the servants of Allah to me.
phrases.explanation: The messenger opens with a demand. The word rendered hand over carries the sense of delivering and of sending along with him, so the demand is to release the servants of God and let them go with him. The reports agree that the servants are the Children of Israel, and one asks why Pharaoh holds a free people as slaves. Some take the words as addressed to Pharaoh, others as a call to the servants themselves.

phrases.translation: I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you
phrases.explanation: Trustworthy here means trusted with the revelation and the message given to him for them. He is not asking for anything of his own, and his honesty is the ground of his demand. The phrase also answers the suspicion that a messenger might come for his own gain. Moses presents himself as one who will not cheat them of what God has entrusted to him.

phrases.translation: And do not be arrogant with Allah.
phrases.explanation: The demand is followed by a prohibition. They are not to exalt themselves above God, which is explained as insolence and excess toward their Lord, leading to disbelief and disobedience. One report reads it as inventing things about God. The prohibition addresses the people as a whole, not only their king, since the messenger speaks to them all and warns them together.

phrases.translation: I have certainly come to you with a compelling proof
phrases.explanation: The proof is a demonstration clear to anyone who considers it. It establishes that what Moses calls them to is true and that he speaks with authority from God. The verse does not describe the proof here, since the signs given to Moses are already known. The claim matters for the argument, because a clear proof puts the hearers under obligation and removes the excuse of ignorance.

phrases.translation: And indeed, I seek refuge with my Lord and your Lord
phrases.explanation: Moses asks his Lord for protection against them, and he names Him as Lord of both sides. The words put the dispute under God's authority rather than under Pharaoh's. Seeking refuge is not a sign of weakness in a messenger but a recognition of where safety lies. The same Lord who sent him is able to guard him from what they intend.

phrases.translation: so you do not stone me ˹to death˺
phrases.explanation: The reports disagree about what stoning means here. Some take it as reviling with the tongue, including the charge that he was a sorcerer. Some take it as stoning with stones, and some as killing. The plain sense is preferred, that Moses sought refuge from every kind of harm they could do him, whether by words or by hands. All the reported meanings fall under that protection, so the verse covers insult and violence alike.

phrases.translation: ˹But˺ if you do not believe me, then let me be.”
phrases.explanation: The messenger asks for one thing only, to be left alone. If they will not accept him as truthful, they should at least let him go his way without being attacked by word or hand. The verse shows the limit of his demand. He does not ask for power or payment, and he does not threaten them, since the matter belongs to God. One report sums it up as simply letting him go.

phrases.translation: Ultimately, he cried out to his Lord, “These are a wicked people!”
phrases.explanation: The story reaches its turning point. Moses calls on his Lord after they called him a liar, refused to believe, would not release the servants of God and wanted to kill him. His complaint is short. He does not ask for their destruction in so many words, he simply states what they are, a criminal people, and this is explained as meaning that they associated partners with God and disbelieved. The answer comes at once.

phrases.translation: ˹Allah responded,˺ “Leave with My servants at night,
phrases.explanation: Something is left unstated in the verse, and what is supplied is that his Lord answered him and told him to set out. The servants are the Children of Israel, those who had believed him and followed him, not those among them who had denied him. The command is to travel by night, before morning. The answer to the complaint is rescue rather than argument, and it comes as soon as Moses calls.

phrases.translation: for you will surely be pursued
phrases.explanation: God tells Moses at the outset that Pharaoh and his people will follow them out of the land. The escape is not a secret that will last, and the pursuit is part of the plan. The warning keeps the messenger from treating the departure as the end of the matter. It also prepares for the sea and for the drowning that the next verse announces.

phrases.translation: And leave the sea parted,
phrases.explanation: Moses is told to leave the sea as it is after he crosses. The reports explain that he wanted to strike it again with his staff so that it would close behind him for fear of pursuit, and that he was stopped. The word describing the sea is disputed. Some take it to mean the sea left in the state it was in, a road. Others take it as smooth and easy to cross, or dry and hard underfoot.

phrases.translation: for they are certainly an army bound to drown.”
phrases.explanation: The closing words name the end of the pursuit. Pharaoh and his people are a host that will be drowned, and this is taken as God's own statement of what awaits them. The sea that opened for the Israelites closes on their pursuers. The verse gives the reason Moses could leave the water standing, since the army behind him was already marked for destruction.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine˺ how many gardens and springs the tyrants left behind
phrases.explanation: The verse invites the hearer to picture what was abandoned. Pharaoh and his people left gardens and springs after they were drowned, and the gardens are identified as orchards and the springs as waters that gushed through their grounds. It adds that they also left standing crops in their fields, which the next verse takes up. The point is the suddenness of the loss, since wealth that seemed secure was left behind when they were destroyed.

phrases.translation: as well as ˹various˺ crops and splendid residences
phrases.explanation: The list continues with crops and with a noble station. The station is explained as a place where they used to stand, a distinguished spot, and the reports differ over why it is called noble. Some say it means the pulpits, since kings and rulers were raised on them. Others say it is called noble for its beauty and splendour, and one report simply renders it as beautiful.

phrases.translation: and luxuries which they fully enjoyed
phrases.explanation: The last item in the list is the comfort they lived in. The phrase is explained as a bounty in which they took delight, enjoyed themselves and lived at ease. The reciters differed over one word in it. Most read it as taking delight, which is preferred, while a few read it as insolent and exultant. Either way the verse describes people whose enjoyment ended when they were driven out, until the sea took them.

phrases.translation: So it was. And We awarded it ˹all˺ to another people
phrases.explanation: The brief sentence draws a line under the story. What was done to those who denied Moses was done deliberately, and their holdings passed to another people after their destruction. The other people are said to be the Children of Israel. The gardens, springs, fields and homes changed hands, so that the punishment is shown as complete, taking both their lives and the wealth they had gathered.

phrases.translation: Neither heaven nor earth wept over them,
phrases.explanation: The verse measures the loss by what did not happen. Heaven and earth did not weep over Pharaoh and his people when they drowned. It is reported that the weeping of heaven is the redness of its horizons, and that when a believer dies his place of prayer on earth and the gate in heaven through which his deeds rose weep over him. The people of Pharaoh left no accepted deed and no trace of worship, so nothing wept.

phrases.translation: nor was their fate delayed
phrases.explanation: No respite was given them. They were not held back from the punishment that came upon them but were hastened into it, since they had brought God's anger on themselves. The drowning came at its appointed moment and could not be postponed. The verse closes the account of Pharaoh by leaving no opening for a second chance.

phrases.translation: And We certainly delivered the Children of Israel
phrases.explanation: After the destruction of their enemy, the Children of Israel are named as the ones rescued. The rescue is credited to God, not to Moses or to their own planning. The verse begins the account of what they were saved from, and that account runs into the next two verses. Their deliverance stands beside the drowning in the same story, so that the same event is judgement for one people and mercy for another.

phrases.translation: from the humiliating torment
phrases.explanation: The punishment they were saved from was the one Pharaoh and his people used to inflict on them, and the word describes it as humiliating and debasing. One report names the specific form it took, the killing of their sons and the sparing of their women. The verse does not dwell on the details. It names the humiliation so that the deliverance is understood as a lifting of disgrace, not merely an escape from pain.

phrases.translation: of Pharaoh. He was truly a tyrant, a transgressor
phrases.explanation: The verse attaches the torment to Pharaoh by name, restating the humiliating punishment as a substitute for it. He is described as haughty and as one of the transgressors. Haughty is explained as exalting himself above his Lord, and transgressor as one who oversteps limits that were not his to cross. He went beyond the bounds in his disbelief and in his arrogance, so that the title fits him exactly.

phrases.translation: And indeed, We chose the Israelites knowingly above the others
phrases.explanation: God chose the Children of Israel above the peoples of their time, with knowledge on His part of what He was choosing. The choosing was not a general superiority over every nation for all time. The reports explain that every age has its own world, and that they were chosen above those around them in the days of Moses. The choice belongs to the favour God showed them, not to a claim they could make for themselves.

phrases.translation: And We showed them signs in which there was a clear test
phrases.explanation: The signs given to the Israelites were also a trial. The reports differ over what kind of trial it was. One holds that God tested them with His favours, naming the rescue from their enemy, the parting of the sea, the cloud that shaded them and the food sent down. Another holds that He tested them with good and evil together. Nothing in the verse limits it to one kind, since both reached them.

phrases.translation: Indeed, these ˹Meccans˺ say
phrases.explanation: The surah turns back to the Quraysh. God reports what they say to the Prophet, and the speakers are identified as the polytheists of his own people. Their words come in the next two verses. The report is set here as a contrast to the deliverance just described, so that the denial of the resurrection is heard against the history of a people whom God had rescued and favoured.

phrases.translation: “There is nothing beyond our first death, and we will never be resurrected
phrases.explanation: The claim is put in their own words. There is only the death they die and no raising afterwards. By this they denied the resurrection, the reward and the punishment together, since a denial of rising again removes both. One report attributes the words to the polytheists of the Arabs generally, explaining the last part as a denial that they would ever be raised. The verse states the position that the surah goes on to answer.

phrases.translation: Bring ˹back˺ our forefathers, if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: The challenge is a demand for proof on their own terms. They ask the Prophet to bring back their forefathers who have already died, if he is truthful that God will raise the dead after they have decayed in their graves. It is noted that the Prophet is addressed alone while the words are meant for all who hear, as in other verses that speak to him on behalf of others.

phrases.translation: Are they superior to the people of Tubba’ and those before them?
phrases.explanation: The question compares the Quraysh with earlier nations and expects the answer no. The people of Tubba' are identified as Tubba' the Ḥimyarite. The reports about him are mixed. One says he was a king from Ḥimyar who marched with armies as far as Samarkand. Others report that he was called a righteous man, that his people were censured but not he, and that he clothed the Ka'ba.

phrases.translation: We destroyed them ˹all˺, ˹for˺ they were truly wicked
phrases.explanation: God destroyed those earlier nations, and the reason given is their criminality and their disbelief in their Lord. The verse turns the comparison into a warning, since the Quraysh are not better than the peoples destroyed before them and cannot expect to be spared while they do the same. A grammatical point is also noted, that the sentence is read as a fresh statement carrying the sense of a condition.

phrases.translation: We did not create the heavens and the earth and everything in between for sport
phrases.explanation: The verse denies that creation is a game. The heavens and the earths and everything between them were not made in play, that is, without purpose or seriousness. The statement is kept general here and expanded in the next verse, where the purpose is named. The denial prepares for the argument about the resurrection, since a creation without purpose would need no judgement and no return.

phrases.translation: We only created them for a purpose,
phrases.explanation: Creation is for a purpose, and the purpose is truth, without which the order could not stand. God did not create people to live as long as He wills and then perish without being tried by command and prohibition and without requital. The creation exists so that the obedient are rewarded and the disobedient are answered. The verse ties the making of the world to the judgement announced earlier in the surah.

phrases.translation: but most of these ˹pagans˺ do not know
phrases.explanation: Most of the polytheists do not know that God created the world for them and for a purpose. Because they deny the return, they do not fear punishment for what displeases Him and do not hope for reward for good they might do. The verse makes their ignorance the reason for their behaviour. It also explains why they mocked the warning and demanded their forefathers be brought back, since they did not expect any accounting.

phrases.translation: Surely the Day of ˹Final˺ Decision is the time appointed for all—
phrases.explanation: The Day of Decision is the day God judges between His creatures for the good and evil they did in this life, rewarding the doer of good with good and the doer of evil with evil. The verse says it is the appointed time for them all, the moment fixed for gathering every one of them. The word carries the sense of a promise kept on a set date, so that the denial of the Quraysh cannot postpone it.

phrases.translation: the Day no kith or kin will be of benefit to another whatsoever,
phrases.explanation: On that day the ties that people relied on will not help. A relative will not ward anything off from a relative, and a friend will not shield a friend from the punishment that has come from God. The word covers both kin and close friend. The verse strips away the support that people counted on in this life, where family and friendship could soften a sentence or share a burden.

phrases.translation: nor will they be helped
phrases.explanation: They will not help one another either, and no one will be able to shelter another from what has struck him, as people did in the world. One report describes the day as one on which all bonds are cut and people are left with their deeds alone, the one whose deeds are good rejoicing and the one whose deeds are evil wretched. Help comes from God alone, and the next verse names those who receive it.

phrases.translation: except those shown mercy by Allah.
phrases.explanation: The exception opens a way through the closed scene. Those on whom God has mercy are not left without help. A dispute among the grammarians is reported about how the exception is attached to the sentence, some making it a substitute and others taking it as a new beginning, and one view explains it as the one permitted to intercede. The reading adopted is that the person shown mercy will intercede for others with his Lord.

phrases.translation: He is truly the Almighty, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: The two names close the verse and explain the exception. God is Almighty in His punishment of His enemies, and Most Merciful toward those He protects and those who obey Him. The pairing keeps the passage from becoming only threat. The same God who judges without being resisted also shows mercy to whom He wills, and the surah has already named mercy as the reason the messengers were sent.

phrases.translation: Surely ˹the fruit of˺ the tree of Zaqqûm
phrases.explanation: The tree is named, and it is identified as the tree that grows in the bottom of the Fire, made into food for its people. The word for sinner here means the one whose sin is disbelief, rather than every lesser fault. One report says that if a single drop of it were sent down to this world it would spoil people's livelihood. Another tells of a man who kept misreading the verse as food of the orphan until he was corrected.

phrases.translation: will be the food of the evildoer
phrases.explanation: The sinner is the one who eats from that tree. Some identified him as Abū Jahl, the opponent who was killed at Badr, though the wording of the verse is general and covers every disbeliever. The food is not described here, only assigned. The following verses describe what it does when it is eaten, so this verse serves as the sentence before the description of the punishment.

phrases.translation: Like molten metal, it will boil in the bellies
phrases.explanation: The food of the tree is compared to molten metal boiling inside the body. The comparison is explained as lead or silver melted in fire until its heat reaches its limit and its glow becomes intense against blackness. The reports describe the metal as dregs of oil or thick water. One report tells of a man who melted gold and silver to show his listeners what it resembles. The reciters read the verb two ways, and both are accepted.

phrases.translation: like the boiling of hot water
phrases.explanation: The comparison is repeated to make the heat concrete. The liquid boils in the bellies of the wretched like water heated until it reaches the utmost. The word means water so intensely heated that its heat has reached its limit, and it takes the form of a passive description even though it means heated. The verse adds one more image to the punishment rather than a new fact.

phrases.translation: ˹It will be said,˺ “Seize them and drag them
phrases.explanation: On the Day of Resurrection the command is given to seize the sinner and drive him forward. The verb means pushing and pulling someone from behind, and an old poem is cited where the same word describes a man being dragged along. The command is addressed to those who carry it out, and the verse does not name them. The picture is one of force, with no dignity left for the one being moved toward the fire.

phrases.translation: into the depths of the Hellfire
phrases.explanation: The destination is the middle of the blazing fire. The word means the midst of the Fire, so the command is to bring him to its centre where the heat is worst. The verse does not describe what happens once he arrives, since the next verse adds the pouring of boiling water over his head. The order of the sentences follows the punishment step by step, from seizing to dragging to arriving.

phrases.translation: Then pour over their heads the torment of boiling water.”
phrases.explanation: The next command adds a further stage. Boiling water is poured over the head of the sinner, and the verse calls it the punishment of boiling water because it is part of what he is punished with. The water is the heated water already described, the same liquid that melts what is inside the body and the skin. Pouring it on the head shows that the torment reaches the most exposed part of a person first.

phrases.translation: ˹The wicked will be told,˺ “Taste this.
phrases.explanation: It is said to the wretched sinner: taste this. The words are addressed to him in the middle of his punishment, and some reports place the whole passage in the story of Abū Jahl. Taste is used here because the punishment is something the man must experience for himself, not merely see or hear about. The sentence is short and final, and the next phrase turns it into a rebuke.

phrases.translation: You mighty, noble one
phrases.explanation: The words are not a compliment. They quote what the man used to say about himself, and one report has Abū Jahl boast that no one between the two mountains was mightier or nobler than he. God returns the boast to him while he is being dragged into the fire. Where is that might now, and why does it not ward off the punishment? The verse leaves him with the titles he chose and no power to use them.

phrases.translation: This is truly what you ˹all˺ used to doubt.”
phrases.explanation: The rebuke ends with the thing itself. This punishment is what they used to doubt in the world and dispute over, and they now meet it directly. The word means doubting and disputing, not simple ignorance. The verse closes the scene in the fire by tying it back to the argument of the surah, where the Quraysh denied the resurrection and demanded proof. What they demanded to see has arrived, and there is no room to argue.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place
phrases.explanation: The scene changes to the other group. Those who feared God by doing what He commanded and avoiding what He forbade will be in a place safe from illness, hardship, grief and loss. The word for place is read in two ways, one suggesting a dwelling and the other a standing place, and both are correct. One report sums it up as safety from Satan, hardship and grief.

phrases.translation: amid Gardens and springs
phrases.explanation: The verse explains what the secure place is. It is gardens and springs, the gardens being orchards and the springs being water that rises and flows at the foot of the trees. The phrase clarifies the one before it, so that the safety promised is not abstract but a settled life in a place of fruit and water. The scene answers the gardens and springs that Pharaoh's people left behind.

phrases.translation: dressed in fine silk and rich brocade,
phrases.explanation: The righteous are clothed in two kinds of silk. One is explained as a thin, fine brocade and the other as a thick, coarse brocade, and one report confirms the second as the coarser cloth. The verse does not use the word garment, since the verb already makes clear what they wear. The clothing continues the description of honour begun with the gardens and springs, adding what the inhabitants wear to where they live.

phrases.translation: facing one another
phrases.explanation: They sit facing one another, and each has his face turned toward the others and none looks at the back of another's neck. The detail describes a gathering where everyone is equally placed, with no one seated behind anyone else. It also suggests ease and openness among the people of the garden. Reports on this were given earlier in the commentary, and are not repeated here.

phrases.translation: So it will be. And We will pair them to maidens with gorgeous eyes
phrases.explanation: The honour shown to the righteous continues. As they were given gardens and silk, they are given spouses from among the wide-eyed maidens, described as pure in whiteness. One report took the word to mean that the gaze is bewildered, and this is disputed, since the word in Arabic means whiteness. Another report describes them as white and wide-eyed, and notes a different reading of the phrase. The Arabic sense is the one adopted.

phrases.translation: There they will call for every fruit in serenity
phrases.explanation: In the garden they ask for every kind of fruit they want and are given it, secure that it will not run out or be cut off. The contrast is drawn with the fruit of this world, which people eat while fearing its harm and its end. The safety is explained as freedom from death, from afflictions and from Satan. The verse turns the earlier picture of gardens and springs into daily life, where want is answered and nothing good is lost.

phrases.translation: There they will never taste death, beyond the first death.
phrases.explanation: The people of the garden will not die again after the first death they died in this world. The grammarians argued over the word rendered beyond, some taking it to mean other than, which reverses the sense. That reading is rejected, since God has made them safe from death once they enter. The word is explained as carrying the sense of after, a usage supported with examples from the Arabs. The first death is the only one they taste.

phrases.translation: And He will protect them from the punishment of the Hellfire—
phrases.explanation: The protection is God's own act, and He kept them from the punishment of the fire as a favour to them. He had not punished them for the sins they committed in the world, and had it not been for that bounty the punishment would have reached them. The verse turns the safety of the righteous into a gift rather than a wage. The next verse names it as grace and calls the outcome the great triumph.

phrases.translation: as ˹an act of˺ grace from your Lord.
phrases.explanation: The safety of the righteous is called a bounty from their Lord, given to them and not earned by right. God did not punish them for what they had done before, and without this favour the fire would have struck them. The phrase keeps the mercy of God at the centre of the reward. Nothing in the verse suggests that their deeds created a claim, only that God chose to spare them and to honour them.

phrases.translation: That is ˹truly˺ the ultimate triumph
phrases.explanation: The comment closes with a verdict. What the righteous are given is the great victory, the success they sought in the world through their deeds, their obedience and their fear of God, by which they kept His commands and avoided what He forbade. The word describes a winning that cannot be reversed, since it is settled in the garden and protected from loss. The surah has shown the two ends side by side, and this phrase names the better one.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have made this ˹Quran˺ easy in your own language ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.explanation: God tells the Prophet that He has made the recitation of the Quran easy in his own tongue, so that the people he is sent to can hear it in the language they understand. The ease is in the tongue, the words flowing for the one who recites them. One report says God made his tongue fluent with it.

phrases.translation: so perhaps they will be mindful
phrases.explanation: The purpose is stated plainly. The Quran is made easy so that the polytheists may take its lessons and proofs to heart, be warned by its admonitions, think about its signs when it is recited to them, and return to obedience once the truth is clear. The word expresses hope from the side of the hearers, since the ease removes their excuse. What remains is whether they will be mindful, and the next verse says that the matter is left to wait.

phrases.translation: Wait then! They too are certainly waiting
phrases.explanation: The surah ends where the warning began. The Prophet is told to wait for the help of his Lord against the polytheists of Quraysh. They for their part are waiting for him to be overcome, and the reports explain the word as simply waiting. The symmetry is the point, since both sides wait, but only one has God's promise. The verse leaves the dispute open in time and certain in outcome, and the surah closes on that expectation.
